# Results — Study 367 (Closed-End Fund Discount)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Does buying closed-end funds
at a deep **discount to NAV** pay you to wait? True per-fund daily NAV is not free on
yfinance, so we build a **transparent NAV proxy**: each CEF is mapped to a published
benchmark for its mandate (an S&P-500 fund → SPY, a utilities fund → XLU, …) and the proxy
discount is the fund's price measured **relative to** that benchmark, demeaned per fund. We
sort funds by proxy-discount each month and test the widest-discount tercile against the
narrowest. Offline & deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — 18 long-listed US equity CEFs + 5 benchmark ETFs (public, no key) |
| Window | 1995-01-03 → 2026-06-18 (**7,918** trading days; **31.5** years; **377** monthly rebalances) |
| NAV proxy | `log(price) − log(benchmark)`, demeaned per fund; **PROXY** for the true price/NAV discount |
| Signal | each month, rank funds by proxy-discount; **long** widest-discount tercile, **short** narrowest |
| Entry / costs | 1-month execution lag (discount at close of *t* earns *t+1*); 20 bps one-way × 2.0 turnover/mo |

> **Proxy + survivorship caveats (named on the Signal axis).** (1) The discount here is a
> *proxy*: price relative to a benchmark, not the fund's reported NAV — it captures the
> price-vs-mandate gap that the true discount mostly drives, but it also absorbs any genuine
> NAV/benchmark tracking error. (2) The 18-name basket is **surviving** CEFs only; funds that
> stayed cheap and liquidated are absent, which biases a discount-reversion test *toward*
> finding an effect. Both caveats travel with the Signal stamp: we read the proxy long-short
> as **real on this tape**, but flag that survivorship and the proxy construction inflate the
> apparent magnitude — and the modern-era sub-sample (below) already shows the edge fading.

## The signal — widest-discount minus narrowest, monthly

1-month entry lag, equal-weighted within each tercile. Welch *t* is the monthly mean vs zero;
the bootstrap *p* is a circular block-bootstrap (6-month blocks, 20,000 draws) two-sided null.

| portfolio | n months | mean / mo | ann. mean | win-rate | Welch *t* | boot *p* | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Long-short** (widest − narrowest tercile) | 377 | **+0.550%** | **+6.60%** | 56% | **+3.72** | 0.002 | **0.66** |
| **Long-only** (widest − equal-weight universe) | 377 | +0.253% | +3.03% | 55% | +2.89 | 0.012 | 0.52 |

The long-short proxy-discount spread is **+6.6%/yr at Welch *t* = 3.72** — statistically real
on this tape and clearing the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar. It is **not** a market-beta artefact (β to
SPY ≈ **−0.003**, monthly alpha **+0.55%**), and it is **not** mechanical: re-running the sort
with the discounts **shuffled across funds** each month collapses the spread to **+0.006% ±
0.13%/mo (p ≈ 0.00)** — the ranking, not the construction, carries it.

## Costs and the short leg — where it gets fragile

| | value |
|---|--:|
| Gross long-short | +6.60% / yr |
| Net @ 20 bps one-way × 2.0 turnover/mo | **+1.80% / yr** |
| Break-even cost (one-way) | **27.5 bps** |

A long-short that rebalances both sleeves monthly turns over ~2× one-way per month; at 20 bps
that is 480 bps/yr of friction, cutting the **6.6% gross to 1.8% net**. Worse, the spread's
**short leg is the narrowest-discount CEFs** — small, illiquid, **hard-to-borrow** closed-end
funds whose borrow cost and availability are exactly the binding constraint a backtest ignores.
The long-only version (no shorting) keeps only **+3.0%/yr gross** and a Sharpe of 0.52.

## Robustness — flat in the cut, but fading in time

| tercile fraction q | n | ann. mean | Welch *t* | boot *p* | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.25 (quartiles) | 377 | +9.74% | 4.34 | 0.001 | 0.77 |
| **0.33** (terciles) | 377 | +6.60% | 3.72 | 0.002 | 0.66 |
| 0.40 | 377 | +6.10% | 3.91 | 0.001 | 0.70 |

| sub-period | n | ann. mean | Welch *t* | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **first half** (1995–2010) | 188 | **+10.64%** | **3.41** | 0.86 |
| **second half** (2011–2026) | 189 | **+2.57%** | **1.56** | 0.39 |

The signal is stable across tercile cuts, but it **decays sharply with time**: a 10.6%/yr,
*t* = 3.4 effect in 1995–2010 falls to 2.6%/yr at **t = 1.56 (below the bar)** in 2011–2026.
That decay — alongside the cost drag and the hard-to-borrow short leg — is what makes it
**FRAGILE**, not investable: the in-sample edge that funds the verdict is largely a pre-2010
phenomenon.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic panel of 18 funds whose log-discount is a mean-reverting AR(1) and whose
forward returns carry a *known* edge proportional to (−discount):

| planted edge | n months | ann. mean | Welch *t* | boot *p* | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (discount carries no return info) | 360 | −0.34% | **−0.19** | 0.846 | −0.03 |
| **0.30** (large planted edge) | 360 | +107.07% | **+48.57** | 0.000 | 8.87 |

With **no** planted edge the sort sits at **t = −0.19** — it does **not** manufacture
significance from noise. A large planted edge drives **t = 48.6**. The harness is unbiased:
it banks an edge that exists and finds nothing when none does — so the **real-tape *t* = 3.72
is a property of the data, not the machine.**

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL (proxy; survivorship-caveated).** The proxy long-short discount spread is
  **+6.6%/yr at Welch *t* = 3.72** (block-bootstrap *p* = 0.002), market-neutral (β ≈ 0),
  placebo-clean (shuffled-discount spread ≈ 0), and stable across tercile cuts — it clears the
  *t* ≥ 2 bar on the real tape. **But** it is a *proxy* discount and rests on a **surviving**
  CEF basket, both of which inflate the magnitude, and the effect **fades to *t* = 1.56**
  post-2010. Real on this tape, with the caveats named.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Gross +6.6%/yr becomes **+1.8%/yr** after 20 bps × monthly
  two-leg turnover (break-even **27.5 bps**), the short leg needs **hard-to-borrow** illiquid
  CEFs, capacity is tiny (18 small funds), and the edge is **mostly pre-2010**. Survives on
  paper, undeployable at scale.
- **"Pays you to wait?" — CONFIRMED (with a catch).** The folklore is genuinely real on the
  proxy: deep-discount funds *do* out-earn as the discount mean-reverts. The catch is that the
  payment is small, costs-sensitive, short-constrained, and fading — a real effect you can
  measure but can barely bank.
